article_units.name: The Human Body and Movement in Physical Activity and Sport
article_units.subtitle: Anatomy, physiology, movement analysis, training and the use of data in sport.

lessons.title: The Skeleton: Structure and Functions
lessons.description: Bones of the skeleton, joint types and the six functions the skeletal system provides for movement.

lessons.title: Muscles and Antagonistic Pairs
lessons.description: Major muscles, agonist and antagonist roles, and isotonic and isometric contractions in sporting actions.

lessons.title: Synovial Joints and Types of Movement
lessons.description: Hinge and ball-and-socket joints, joint structures that prevent injury, and movement at major joints.

lessons.title: The Cardiovascular System and Exercise
lessons.description: Heart structure, the pathway of blood, blood vessels and how the cardiovascular system responds to exercise.

lessons.title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
lessons.description: The pathway of air, mechanics of breathing and how gas exchange occurs in the alveoli during exercise.

lessons.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Exercise
lessons.description: Energy equations, EPOC and how recovery methods help the body return to a resting state.

lessons.title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise
lessons.description: Immediate, short-term and long-term physiological adaptations, including hypertrophy and bradycardia.

lessons.title: Lever Systems and Mechanical Advantage
lessons.description: First, second and third class levers in sport, and how mechanical advantage is calculated and applied.

lessons.title: Planes and Axes of Movement
lessons.description: Frontal, transverse and sagittal planes and axes applied to somersaults, twists and cartwheels.

lessons.title: Health, Fitness and the Components of Fitness
lessons.description: Definitions of health and fitness and the ten components needed for sporting performance.

lessons.title: Fitness Testing: Procedures and Validity
lessons.description: Standard fitness tests, what they measure and the limitations of test data for sporting performers.

lessons.title: Principles of Training: SPORT and FITT
lessons.description: Specificity, progressive overload, reversibility, tedium and the FITT principles applied to programmes.

lessons.title: Methods of Training
lessons.description: Continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight, plyometric and static stretching matched to fitness aims.

lessons.title: Optimising Training and Preventing Injury
lessons.description: Heart rate zones, one rep max, altitude training, seasonal aspects and injury prevention strategies.

lessons.title: Warm Up and Cool Down
lessons.description: Components, physiological benefits and psychological role of warming up and cooling down.

lessons.title: Using Data in Physical Activity and Sport
lessons.description: Collecting, presenting and interpreting qualitative and quantitative data from training and testing.

article_units.name: Socio-Cultural Influences and Wellbeing in Physical Activity and Sport
article_units.subtitle: Sports psychology, society, ethics and the role of physical activity in health and wellbeing.

lessons.title: Skill, Ability and the Classification of Skills
lessons.description: Skill versus ability, the four classification continuums and matching them to sporting examples.

lessons.title: Goal Setting and SMART Targets
lessons.description: Performance and outcome goals and how SMART targets are used to improve sporting performance.

lessons.title: Information Processing in Sport
lessons.description: Input, decision making, output and feedback applied to skills and game situations.

lessons.title: Guidance for Beginners and Elite Performers
lessons.description: Visual, verbal, manual and mechanical guidance and when each is most effective.

lessons.title: Feedback in Sporting Performance
lessons.description: Positive, negative, intrinsic, extrinsic and knowledge of results or performance feedback in sport.

lessons.title: Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory
lessons.description: The relationship between arousal and performance and how stress management techniques control arousal.

lessons.title: Personality, Aggression and Motivation
lessons.description: Introvert and extrovert types, direct and indirect aggression, and intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation.

lessons.title: Engagement Patterns and Social Groups
lessons.description: How gender, age, race, religion, family and disability shape participation in physical activity.

lessons.title: Commercialisation: Sponsorship and the Media
lessons.description: The golden triangle of sport, sponsorship and media, and the impacts on performers and audiences.

lessons.title: Technology in Sport
lessons.description: Positive and negative impacts of technology on performers, officials, audiences and the integrity of sport.

lessons.title: Conduct of Performers in Sport
lessons.description: Etiquette, sportsmanship, gamesmanship and the contract to compete in modern competition.

lessons.title: Performance Enhancing Drugs and Blood Doping
lessons.description: Categories of prohibited substances, blood doping and the advantages and disadvantages for performers.

lessons.title: Spectator Behaviour and Hooliganism
lessons.description: The positive and negative effects of crowds and the strategies used to combat hooliganism.

lessons.title: Physical, Emotional and Social Wellbeing
lessons.description: How participation in sport supports physical health, mental health and social wellbeing.

lessons.title: Sedentary Lifestyle, Obesity and Somatotypes
lessons.description: Consequences of inactivity, how obesity affects performance, and ectomorph, mesomorph and endomorph body types.

lessons.title: Energy, Diet, Nutrition and Hydration
lessons.description: Daily energy needs, the role of macronutrients and how dehydration affects sporting performance.

lessons.title: Interpreting Data on Participation and Performance
lessons.description: Reading tables, bar charts, line graphs and pie charts that describe sport, participation and wellbeing.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name a single muscle as 'the' agonist for a movement without specifying the joint, the direction of movement and which muscle is acting as the antagonist. Content should always frame agonist/antagonist as a pair, anchored to a joint and a phase of movement (e.g. biceps agonist, triceps antagonist during elbow flexion in a bicep curl up phase).
common_misconceptions.source: AQA Inside Assessment — Physical Education (https://www.aqa.org.uk/professional-development/inside-assessment/bringing-assessment-to-life/physical-education) and AQA subject-specific vocabulary guidance (https://filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/pe/AQA-8582-VOCAB.PDF)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mis-order Load, Fulcrum and Effort or fail to label the effort and load arms when asked to draw a lever, losing marks on routine 2- and 3-mark questions. Mark schemes require the LFE order to be visibly correct on the diagram.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE PE Paper 1 specimen mark scheme (https://filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/pe/AQA-85821-SMS.PDF)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students identify a sport as 'aerobic' or 'anaerobic' without justifying using duration and intensity. The spec explicitly requires justification using intensity-and-duration evidence (e.g. 'sprinting <10s, very high intensity, insufficient oxygen → anaerobic').

Students confuse 'open' (environment changes — football pass under pressure) with 'simple' or 'gross'. Reinforce that open/closed is about predictability of environment, not body parts used or complexity. Skill classifications are continuums, not binary tick-boxes.

common_misconceptions.topic: Mark scheme demands on extended response
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students answer 9-mark 'evaluate' questions one-sided. To reach full marks they must consider both sides of the argument and apply knowledge to a sporting context, not just describe.

student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Evaluate: Students often produce one-sided arguments and forget to apply each point to a named sport. Mark schemes are levels-based and reward (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument and (c) consistent sporting application. Encourage 'For X... However Y...' structures with a sporting example anchored to each stem.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Analyse: Students list rather than analyse. Each point should be developed: state the factor, link it to performance, give a sporting example. Avoid bullet-point answers; encourage continuous prose.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Interpret Data: Students copy numbers from the table without saying what they show. Always make a comparison, quote one figure, then explain the sporting implication.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Calculate from Data: Students forget the unit (e.g. bpm, %, seconds) or skip showing working. Mark schemes typically award 1 for working, 1 for the correct figure, 1 for the unit. Always show all three.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — State Two: Students give two near-identical answers (e.g. 'increased heart rate' and 'heart rate goes up'). Mark schemes award once for the same physiological point — the second answer must be qualitatively different.

topic_weighting_notes: Applied anatomy and physiology dominates Paper 1 — every paper carries multi-mark questions on muscles, the cardio-respiratory system and the effects of exercise. Treat Lessons 1–7 as the foundation block and revisit them in worked examples in later lessons (training, warm up, optimising training).

Use of data appears across both papers as 3- and 4-mark questions on tables, bar charts and pie charts. Bake data interpretation into practice questions throughout the build, not just into the dedicated data lessons.

Socio-cultural and ethical issues (commercialisation, PEDs, hooliganism) yield rich 6- and 9-mark questions. These lessons need contemporary, balanced examples with explicit positive and negative impacts framed.

Movement analysis (lever systems, planes and axes) is small in mark weighting but high-value because the questions are predictable. Drill the diagram-labelling steps in flashcards and knowledge checks.
current_spec_changes: From summer 2027 the practical NEA activity list has been updated so that both boys and girls can be assessed in 300 m and 300 m hurdles, aligning with national governing body guidance. This is a practical-assessment change only and does not affect Paper 1 or Paper 2 written content. Source: https://www.aqa.org.uk/news/gcse-pe-specification-updates-for-summer-2027

Specification version 1.7 (11 November 2025) is the current authoritative document. No content additions or removals affect the theory papers for the 2026 series. Source: https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/physical-education/gcse/physical-education-8582/specification
pedagogical_notes: EEF guidance on retrieval practice: the active attempt to recall is what builds long-term memory; quizzes must include a delay between learning and recall, balance challenge with success, and provide feedback. Knowledge checks and flashcards in this build must be true retrieval tasks (not just re-reading) and should mix anatomy, training and socio-cultural content to force students to discriminate between related concepts. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-not-another-quiz-refining-retrieval-practice

EEF cognitive science review identifies dual coding (pairing words with diagrams) as a high-utility classroom strategy. PE content is anatomy-heavy: where a diagram would clarify (heart chambers, lever systems, planes/axes, inverted-U graph), the lesson should describe it precisely in text and include a key-fact 'sketch this without looking' retrieval prompt. Free-tier lessons do not embed generated images, so the prose must do the imaging work. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/evidence-reviews/cognitive-science-approaches-in-the-classroom

EEF spaced-practice principle: revisiting material across days outperforms massed practice. Lessons should explicitly cross-reference earlier lessons (e.g. when teaching warm-up, retrieve the cardio-respiratory and muscular adaptations from Lessons 4 and 5). Build deliberate retrieval prompts into key-facts. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-putting-cognitive-science-principles-into-practice

EEF interleaving principle: mixing related topics in retrieval forces students to discriminate. Knowledge checks should not be pure single-topic — Paper 1 lessons should mix anatomy with training, and Paper 2 lessons should mix sports psychology with socio-cultural influences. Source: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/news/eef-blog-the-abc-of-cognitive-science

Glossary terms: PE is terminology-dense (every named bone, muscle, joint, training method, principle and ethical concept needs precise definition). Aim for at least 6 inline glossary terms per lesson; 8–10 is realistic in anatomy lessons. Definitions should be one sentence and reusable across lessons.

Data interpretation: AQA Paper 2 specifically tests use of data. Generate ORIGINAL fictional data tables and graph descriptions in question stems — never reproduce real AQA figures. Use realistic numbers (e.g. 'Sarah's heart rate during a 30-min run: rest 70 bpm, peak 165 bpm, recovery 90 bpm at 5 min'). Include at least one '4 marks — Interpret Data' or '3 marks — Calculate from Data' question in lessons where the topic is amenable (Cardiovascular System, Effects of Exercise, Engagement Patterns, Energy and Diet, plus the two dedicated data lessons). Source: AQA Inside Assessment (https://www.aqa.org.uk/professional-development/inside-assessment/bringing-assessment-to-life/physical-education)

Mark scheme rubric: StudyVault uses Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging on 6- and 9-mark levels-based questions. NEVER use 'Level 1/2/3', 'Nothing worthy of credit' or 'Award X marks for Y'. Phrase mark allocations as '1 mark for X; 1 mark for Y' or 'Up to 3 marks: identification (1), context (1), explanation (1)'. The validator hard-bans the 'Award N marks for' pattern.

Plain-text fields (description, practice_questions[].text/.type/.marks, knowledge_checks[].q, flashcard_questions[].q/.a, glossary_terms[].term/.definition) MUST use plain unicode (apostrophes, en-dashes, em-dashes typed directly). NEVER use HTML entities such as ’, &, – in these fields — entities are only allowed inside content_html, exam_tip_html, conclusion_html.

Copyright: do not include spec codes (8582), paper codes (8582/1, 8582/2), section labels, or AQA's trademark question stems verbatim. Do not write 'Other than X, identify...' style questions that mimic AQA's structure. Do not reproduce AQA mark scheme phrasing. Build generic GCSE-level questions with our 11 registered command-word types.

gaps: Practical NEA (40% of qualification) is teacher-assessed and not addressed by this revision platform. Students are pointed to their school's PE department for activity assessment, drills and the analysis-and-evaluation coursework. The 33 lessons in this plan cover 100% of the assessable theory content for Paper 1 and Paper 2 (60% of the qualification).

From summer 2027 onwards, 300 m and 300 m hurdles are added as practical NEA activities for both genders. This is a practical change only and does not affect the theory content of the lessons in this plan.
